blindSummary:
This country is one of the few in the world that criminalises gender expression as such — a high-danger destination for trans visitors. All 13 states/provinces and the federal territory prohibit "a man posing as a woman" under religious law (up to 3 years in jail, a fine, and caning). These laws technically bind only adherents of the state religion, but the enforcement climate affects all trans people: religious-enforcement units conduct systematic raids on trans events — tipping off media in advance and sharing detainees' faces with tabloids (public outing and humiliation). Three trans women were killed in fewer than two months in 2019.

The political climate is shifting toward parties that seek to expand religious law (a deputy minister urged labelling LGBT people as promoting "deviant behaviour"; state-backed "rehabilitation" programmes; dating-site blocking). For a foreign trans visitor who does not adhere to the state religion, the religious cross-dressing offence does not apply directly, but being caught in a raided venue, facing the enforcement climate, or being charged under the penal-code provisions on same-sex conduct (up to 20 years plus whipping, which apply to everyone including tourists) are real risks. There is no legal gender recognition.
blindOutOfScope: General crime and compliance with the country's religious law (alcohol rules, dress codes at religious sites) affect adherent and non-adherent travellers in different ways; only trans-specific risk is assessed.

International jurists' commission (July 2020): condemned an order by the religious-affairs minister giving the federal territory's religious administration full licence to carry out its enforcement actions against transgender persons; called for the order to be revoked and for non-discrimination guarantees.

Practical travel guide (updated July 2026): the law, religious-law provisions, court rulings and practical guidance for visitors and residents - penal-code provisions criminalise 'unnatural' sex for anyone regardless of gender or consent (up to 20 years plus whipping), including tourists; state religious-law offences covering male same-sex acts, female same-sex acts and cross-dressing apply only to adherents of the state religion (max 3 years, a fine, 6 strokes of the cane); no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law; the apex court struck down one state/province's religious-offence provision (2021) and 16 provisions of another state/province (2024) on federalism grounds; enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted.

International human-rights organisation (Sept 2014): report that transgender people here are under threat - documents arrests of trans women under religious-law provisions criminalising 'a male person posing as a woman', violence, and a landmark court-of-appeal ruling finding one state/province's law unconstitutional.
blindTangential: The penal-code provisions on same-sex conduct (up to 20 years plus whipping) apply to everyone, visitors included — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
